The AP can be whatever. Set them up as AP and go to town. I use apple airports, because I already had them, but I wouldn't buy them again. No reason to pay for apple when the hardware is very similar to many other devices.

This is overkill. There is no question it is overkill. It is more reliable than clocks in my house. I spend more time maintaining clocks than this convoluted router system.

A step up from this would be a pfSense VM with a Unifi AP, however I believe the learning curve for both the pfSense and Unifi is going to be higher than OpenWRT and apple APs. A setup like this will require 2 NICs in your ESXi server or some VLAn tagging at the switch level. The other issue you might run into with visualizing a firewall is you might need to spoof the MAC address on the virtual NIC to get the modem to properly provide an IP to the VM.

PFsense was super easy to set up. I strongly suggest anyone who is interested in doing what I do start with PFsense. OpenWRT has a better interface for my purposes. I haven't done any VLANs, why would you suggest that?

vLANs would be useful if you're running a single NIC on your ESXi host. On the switch you would setup a vLAN for your WAN and LAN networks and assign an access port to the WAN vLAN that you would plug your broadband modem into, and access ports on your LAN vLAN for anything that you want on your LAN network. Next you would setup a vLAN trunk port on your switch that included both the LAN and WAN vLANs for the ESXi host. On the ESXi host you would add the WAN and LAN vLAN IDs to the virtual switch then assign the virtual NICs on pfSense or OpenWRT to the appropriate vLANs. At this point everything plugs into your switch, yet only the pfSense WAN vNIC has access to the broadband modem.

vLANs can also be used to isolate your WiFi network from your wired network, and if your WiFi access point supports it can be used to isolate a guest WiFi network. You can apply more restrictive firewall rules to those networks if desired. For example, I have a guest WiFi network setup that runs on it's own vLAN which does not have access to my home network. It is throttled and only allowed to access ports 80 and 443 on the internet. Everything is plugged into the same switch and is segmented using vLANs.

Short answer, yes on getting your own modem, no on a combined device. Long answer.

  1. Returning equipment: When you return your modem to them, get a receipt and document everything, including the person you returned it to. You will need that later if they claim you never returned your router.
  2. Single point of failure: Buy a separate modem and WiFi router. You will get better performance from both if you get separate items. A combined device is a single point of failure. If your router fails (which happened to me) you will at least still have internet connectivity because you have a modem.
  3. Compatibility: Get a DOCSIS 3.0 or better modem. Plan on spending at least $50 US for a decent modem. Here is a PDF link for compatible modems on TWC. Comcast has a similar list.
  4. Price: You will end up paying off the modem in 5 or more months, given your current rental rate. It pays for itself! This means you will have more money down the road to spend on a better WiFi Router. I would budget at least $125 US for a decent router.
  5. Moving: If you ever move and end up with a different ISP, you will still be able to use your WiFi router, the only thing you need to worry about is the modem.
  6. Security: By having separate devices, your ISP has not ability to control the WiFi router. Comcast combined equipment in their default configuration allows others Comcast customers to use your bandwidth! They have the ability to alter the router configuration as they see fit. You can escape this by owning and configuring your own equipment.
  7. Repairs: If something fails, you are responsible for fixing it, which can be a good thing. You are not dependent on a ill-trained technician to fix your issues or dependent on their schedule. On the bad side, if you are not comfortable with troubleshooting and fixing your own equipment, then you shouldn't be asking the question about buying your own modem. Sorry if that is harsh, but it is reality.

Hope this helps!
